title: Broken Access Control
summary: The OWASP #1 category: bugs that let one authenticated user reach another user's data or an admin's functions. Covers IDOR, missing function-level checks, and why a client-side check is never a control.

slides.markdown:
Broken Access Control has been the [OWASP Top 10](owasp-top-10)'s #1 category since 2021, and it's deceptively simple to describe: a user does something they're authenticated for, but not **authorized** for, and the application lets them anyway.

Unlike [injection](injection-attacks) or [XSS](xss), there's no payload to craft — the "attack" is often just changing a number in a URL. That simplicity is exactly why it's so common: it doesn't take a skilled attacker, just someone curious enough to try.

This topic covers the application-layer *bugs* — IDOR, missing function-level checks, and the client-side-check trap. The authorization *design patterns* meant to prevent these bugs at the architecture level — RBAC, ABAC — live in the next group's [Authorization Models](authorization-models); this topic is about how those designs fail in practice, one missing check at a time.

Two forces pushed Broken Access Control to #1 in the 2021 edition:

- **It's genuinely common.** Access control has to be re-checked on *every single* endpoint that touches user-specific or privileged data — there's no one place to "fix it once." Miss a check on one of two hundred endpoints and that one endpoint is exploitable.
- **Automated scanning got better at finding it.** IDOR and missing-authorization patterns are now flagged systematically by modern testing tools, surfacing bugs that were always present but previously required manual probing to discover.

The practical consequence: this category doesn't get fixed by adding one library or enabling one setting, the way `SameSite` cookies mostly close CSRF. It requires a check to be present and correct at *every* access point, which is exactly why it recurs — a system can be 99% correctly authorized and still ship an exploitable gap on the 1% that was missed.

**IDOR** is the single most common concrete form of broken access control: an endpoint uses a direct, guessable reference — usually a sequential ID — to fetch a resource, and never checks that the requester actually **owns** that resource.

`GET /orders/1234` returns your order. Change the URL to `GET /orders/1235` and if the server only checks "is this a valid order ID and is the requester logged in" — not "does this order belong to *this* requester" — you now see someone else's order: their address, their items, their payment's last four digits.

The bug is almost always the same missing line: the query fetches by ID alone (`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?`) instead of by ID *and* owner (`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?`). Authentication succeeded — the requester really is logged in — but authorization never ran at all.

A second common shape: an **admin-only feature that exists at a URL or API route, but the route itself never verifies the caller is actually an admin** — it relies entirely on the admin UI simply not linking to it for regular users.

`GET /admin/users/export` might power a button that's only rendered for admin accounts in the UI. If the underlying route doesn't independently check the caller's role — trusting that "nobody will guess this URL" — any authenticated user who finds or guesses the route gets the same access an admin would, silently.

This is distinct from IDOR in shape (it's about a *function*, not a specific *record*) but identical in root cause: authorization was designed to live in the UI's routing decisions rather than enforced at the server boundary where the actual request lands.

Both IDOR and missing function-level checks are instances of **privilege escalation**, and the two variants have different blast radii:

- **Horizontal escalation** — reaching another user's data at the *same* privilege level. The IDOR example (user A reading user B's order) is horizontal: neither user is more privileged than the other, but the boundary between their accounts is broken.
- **Vertical escalation** — reaching functionality meant for a *higher* privilege level. The missing admin-route check is vertical: a regular user reaches admin-only capability.

Vertical escalation is generally the more severe finding in a security review, since it doesn't just leak one other user's data, it can grant capabilities (delete any account, export the full user table) that scale to the whole system. But horizontal escalation at scale — an IDOR that lets you iterate `/orders/1` through `/orders/999999` — can be just as damaging in aggregate, since it's a full data breach one sequential request at a time.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a client-side check is not an access control
slides.markdown:
The single most common misconception, and the one that produces most of the bugs above: **anything running in the browser is not a security control**, no matter how convincingly it restricts the UI.

Hiding a "Delete User" button unless `user.role === 'admin'`, disabling a form field for non-owners, or redirecting away from an unauthorized page in client-side JavaScript are all genuinely good **UX** — they guide legitimate users toward what they're allowed to do. None of them are **security**, because the client is entirely under the attacker's control. Anyone can open dev tools, re-enable the hidden button, edit the disabled field, or simply call the underlying API directly with a tool like curl, bypassing the UI altogether.

The rule that actually holds: every access-control decision must be re-validated **server-side**, at the point the request actually lands, using data the server itself trusts — never using anything the client asserts about its own role or permissions.

slides.sectionTitle: An IDOR request walking through the system
slides.markdown:
![Request flow showing an IDOR: authentication passes, the ownership check never runs, and the database returns another user's order](assets/idor-request-flow.svg)

The diagram isolates exactly where the fix belongs: authentication (top) genuinely succeeds, so it's not the broken step. The break is the missing box between authentication and data access — the authorization check that should ask "does this specific resource belong to this specific authenticated user," and never runs at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Hiding a feature in the UI and calling it access controlled
slides.markdown:
A variant of the client-side-check trap specific to feature rollout: a team ships an unfinished or admin-only feature by simply not linking to it anywhere in the UI, reasoning "nobody will find the URL if we don't show a button for it."

This is **security through obscurity applied to access control**, and it fails for a predictable set of reasons: URLs leak through browser history, shared links, referrer headers, JavaScript bundles that reference the route even if no link renders it, and straightforward URL guessing (`/api/v2/users/export` is not a hard guess once `/api/v1/users/list` is known). Automated scanners crawl JavaScript source specifically looking for route strings that never appear as a rendered link.

The fix is identical to the missing function-level check fix: the route itself must enforce the authorization check server-side. "We didn't link to it" is a UX decision, and it provides precisely zero security value on its own.

slides.sectionTitle: Making access control systematic, not per-endpoint
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
Given that access control has to be correct on every single endpoint, the senior-level fix isn't reviewing each one carefully — it's making the *default* safe, so a missed check fails closed rather than open.

- **Centralize the check, don't repeat it.** A shared authorization middleware or decorator (`@require_owner(Order)`) that every sensitive route uses means the ownership logic is written and tested once, not reimplemented — and potentially miswritten — on every route individually.
- **Deny by default.** New routes should require an explicit authorization annotation to be reachable at all, rather than being open by default and requiring someone to remember to add a check. A missing decorator should mean "nobody can access this," not "everybody can."
- **Test access control as a first-class test suite**, not an afterthought — automated tests that assert "user A gets a 404 on user B's resources" across every resource type, run in CI, catch a regression before it ships rather than after a scanner or a bug bounty report finds it.
- **Log authorization denials**, tying this topic back to [logging failures](security-misconfig-logging) — a spike in 403/404s against sequential IDs from one account is exactly the IDOR-probing signal worth alerting on.

The unifying idea: don't trust engineers to remember a check on every endpoint forever. Build a system where forgetting fails safe.
